blocks.text: These are the species of locusts which the sacred translators mention. Many others could be added to them, drawn from the storehouses of the Greeks, if that were the matter in hand. For example, in Aristophanes the τετραπτερυλλίδες [tetrapterullides], so called from their four wings. And [col. 450] the πάρνοπες [parnopes] of the Attic countryside, from whose expulsion, as Pausanias relates in his Attica, Apollo Parnopius was named; just as the κόρνοπες [kornopes] of the Oetaeans gave its name to Hercules Kornopion in Strabo, book 13. And the μάσακες [masakes] and μολουρίδες [molourides] in Nicander's Theriaca, lines 416 and 802. And in Theocritus, Idyll 10, μάντις ἁ καλαμαία [mantis ha kalamaia], which others call ἀρουραία [arouraia], the prophetess of the reeds, or of the fields. So too in Cyprus the Cerynetae called small cicadas καλαμίνδας [kalamindas], as Hesychius attests under Καλαμίς [Kalamis]. But the locust was called not only καλαμαία [kalamaia] but μάντις καλαμαία [mantis kalamaia], because it foretells barrenness to the reeds, that is, the crops. So in Arabic a kind of locust is called جندب [jundab] gindab, which takes its name from جدب [jadb] gidab, that is, a barren year. To these must be added the tryxalis, of which Pliny speaks in book 30, chapter 6: There is an animal like a locust, without wings, which is called TRYXALIS in Greek. It has no Latin name, etc. (I would prefer troxalis, τρωξαλὶς [trōxalis], as it is written by Aelian, History, book 6, chapter 19.) And Dioscorides' ἀσίρακος [asirakos], in the chapter On locusts in book 2 (where some copies wrongly have ἡ ῥιξαχόσκη· [hē rhixachoskē]): a species of locust around Leptis in Africa, ἄπτερος [apteros] and μεγαλόκωλος [megalokōlos], without wings and with long legs, which in Greek is called ὄνος [onos], ass, but in the native tongue of the inhabitants (that is, in Punic) ἀσίρακος [asirakos] ^{(21)}. From this, by the transposition of a single letter, came the Talmudists' אסקרא askra, or iskra, a kind of locust of which the doctors treat in the tractate Cholin, ch. 3, fol. 65a: מאי זחל אמר רבי אסקרא. What is zachal? Rabbi said: Ascra. That is, it is the same kind of locust as the ascra. And the Gloss: זחל מין חגב בלשון ארמי אסקרא ואין לו קרצולים בקטנותו וגדלים לאחר זמן, ZACHAL is a species of locust, called ASKRA in Syriac, which does not have long legs while it is small, but in time they grow. Then indeed it becomes μεγαλόκωλος [megalokōlos], as Dioscorides has it. Yet it is slow in its gait, whence it is called זחל by the Hebrews and ὄνος [onos] by the Greeks. In the Arabic-Syriac-Latin Thesaurus of Thomas a Novaria, for ܐܣܩܪܐ askra is wrongly written ܐܣܩܕܐ askda, and it is rendered in Arabic المذنب [al-mudhannab], the tailed locust. [III, 266] In Hesychius too there are many names of locusts: such as Ἄχηρον· ἀκρίδα, Κρῆτες [Achēron; akrida, Krētes]. (But in Suidas Ἀχήρας [Achēras], or ἀχώρας [achōras], is a kind of worm.) Βρέττανα φοβερὰ, ἀκρὶς μικρὰ ὑπὸ Κρητῶν [Brettana phobera, akris mikra hypo Krētōn]. Likewise, Θυλακοθρὼξ, μῦς, οἱ δὲ ἀκρίς· [Thylakothrōx, mys, hoi de akris], as if it gnawed sacks just as a mouse does. Likewise, Πετηλὶς, ἀκρίς· [Petēlis, akris], from the leaves which it consumes: for πέτηλον [petēlon] is a leaf. Likewise, Ὄρπας· τῆς ἀκρίδος ὁ γόνος, ἔνθεν γὰρ ὀπυίουσιν [Orpas; tēs akridos ho gonos, enthen gar opyiousin] (I read γάρον ποιοῦσιν [garon poiousin]), Orpas, the offspring of the locust, from which they make garum: namely, to drive them away or to destroy them. That this emendation is correct, gather from these words of Democritus in the Geoponica, book 13, chapter 1: Ἀποδιώξεις τὰς ἀκρίδιας, ἐὰν, γάρον ἐξ αὐτῶν σκευάσας, βόθρους ὀρύξῃς, καὶ ταύτας ἐγκαταβρέξῃς τῷ γάρῳ. μεθ᾽ ἡμέρας γὰρ ἐπελθὼν, εὑρήσεις αὐτὰς ἐν τοῖς βόθροις ὕπνῳ βεβαρημένας [Apodiōxeis tas akridias, ean, garon ex autōn skeuasas, bothrous oryxēs, kai tautas enkatabrexēs tō garō. meth' hēmeras gar epelthōn, heurēseis autas en tois bothrois hypnō bebarēmenas]. You will drive away the locusts if, having made garum from them, you dig trenches and soak them with that garum. For when you go there after some days, you will find them in the trenches, heavy with sleep. To the ORPAS of Hesychius the Arabs' عرفان [ʿurfān] orphan alludes, a kind of locust near Medina, of which above ^{c)}).
